Quickstart

Open-source small language model fine-tuning platform

Fine-tune small language models from a base model on your own data.

Start from your documents. BrewSLM writes training pairs and a held-out answer key from your passages with a local or cloud model you choose, then measures the base model with and without those passages, so you know whether retrieval alone is enough before you train. If it isn't, it trains a small model on your machine, and tells you whether the result beat the base model or sits within noise. Then it exports an artifact you can ship and inspect. Existing labelled datasets import too.

documents → training data Q&A pairs plus a held-out answer key, reviewed or accepted
verdict vs the base model paired on the same test rows, with a noise band
local + auditable run locally, inspect every step

Shipped with BrewSLM

Real models and real runs, every number measured

Four builds done end to end in BrewSLM, with the evaluation that went with them, including the result that went the other way.

Sensitive-data tagger on Hugging Face

A DeBERTa-v3 model that finds and locates 30 types of sensitive data with character offsets, trained with no human-labelled training rows. Span F1 0.97 on a 44-text answer key written by the same model that labelled its training data, so it measures agreement with that labeller (0.92 on the 11 texts a person checked); 0.78 on the independent Gretel PII benchmark (500 texts, measured after removing benchmark values that had leaked into the training data); 0.80 on CoNLL-2003 person names (400 texts).

  • TensorGreed/brewslm-sensitive-data-tagger
  • How it was built, step by step

Passage reader for IRS Publication 17 on Hugging Face

Qwen2.5-1.5B fine-tuned to answer from retrieved passages, with every row of its data written by open-weight models running locally, test set included. 0.688 vs 0.570 for the same base model reading the same passages, on 157 questions fixed before scoring. All three training seeds beat that bar. For education only.

  • TensorGreed/brewslm-pub17-passage-reader
  • How it was built, two misses included

Accident-report extractor on Hugging Face

Qwen2.5-1.5B fine-tuned to turn an NTSB aviation accident narrative into a 13-field JSON record, writing null for anything the text doesn't state. 0.959 of fields exactly right vs 0.494 for the base model, on 1,234 held-out reports; all three seeds passed a rule written before training. No language model wrote any of its data. For education only.

  • TensorGreed/brewslm-ntsb-accident-extractor
  • How it was built, misses included

RAG vs fine-tuning on IRS Publication 17

Same 41 held-out questions, same judge: the base model scored 0.17, the base model with retrieved passages 0.73, and a fine-tune on 405 generated pairs 0.02. BrewSLM's pre-training check said not to fine-tune before any training ran.

  • Read the run, failure included
  • When fine-tuning isn't the answer

Academy

Learn the concepts that power the product

BrewSLM promotes the workflow; the Academy is the learning surface. Use it to learn supervised fine-tuning, LoRA, base-model choice, custom dataset shapes, and evaluation before you run the platform on your own domain data.

How a project runs

Documents in, a verdict out, then ship

Each stage is a destination in the workspace (Overview, Data, Train, Results, Ship), and each has an Academy lesson. Importing an existing dataset is covered on Capabilities.

01 Documents

Bring the text the model should know

Upload PDFs and other documents on Data → Sources, or pull a git repository or a website. Cleaning splits them into passages at sentence boundaries; the passages feed both generation and retrieval.

Clean and prepare →

02 Synthetic data

Training data written from your passages

A local model (Ollama) or a cloud API you configure writes question-answer pairs from each passage and one held-out question per passage for the answer key. The documents flow accepts its pairs directly; rows from the synthetic playbooks wait in the review queue, where you reject them by reason in bulk.

Synthetic data and review →

03 Measure first

Is retrieval already enough?

Before training, a judge scores the base model reading your passages on the test split, with the best retrieval settings a sweep can find. When that already answers well, the flow stops before training and says to serve the passages instead.

When fine-tuning isn't the answer →

04 Train

A run on your own GPU

Preflight checks the data and the config, then the Celery worker runs the training script: LoRA by default, full fine-tuning, continued pretraining, distillation or a token-classification head. The bell tracks it.

Training jobs and monitoring →

05 Verdict

Better than the base model, or within noise?

When a run finishes, BrewSLM scores the base model and the trained one on the same held-out rows and compares them row by row. The scorer matches the task shape, and your pass/fail rule set says whether the run is good enough to ship.

Evaluate: rules and failure clusters →

06 Ship

Export, publish, deploy

Package a run as GGUF, ONNX, TensorRT, Hugging Face or Docker, publish a Hugging Face export to the Hub, and track deployed versions with promote and rollback.

Export, deploy and Coach →

Why this matters

What you stop doing once BrewSLM is in your loop

Stop fine-tuning before you've measured

On IRS Publication 17 the base model reading retrieved passages scored 0.73 and a fine-tune scored 0.02. The pre-training check said "don't fine-tune" before any training ran.

Stop trusting one number

The verdict pairs the base and trained model on the same rows and says when a difference is within noise for a test set that size, instead of celebrating a two-point gain.

Stop guessing which metric to trust

Task-aware scorers match the shape: span F1 for taggers, typed field match with nulls for JSON records, per-class F1 for classifiers, a judge for long answers.

Stop losing rows silently

Rejected rows carry a reason, in the review queue and in imports alike. Drop the categories you choose; the counts stay in the record.

Architecture

Three planes, all running on your machine

Data plane

Sources (jsonl / csv / file / hf / kaggle / git / web / plugin) → Introspector → Target mapper → Project's synthetic dataset (JSONL on disk). Imported rows are written as accepted: they skip the review queue and train directly.

Training plane

Prepared manifest → preflight → training job on the Celery worker (LoRA, full, continued pretraining, distillation, token classification) → checkpoints and weights, on the local trainer or an optional cloud-burst backend.

Eval + delivery plane

Task-handler dispatcher (classification / qa / structured extraction / rag / alignment / seq2seq / vision-language / audio / safety / tool calling, with a generic fallback) → verdict against the base model → export formats (GGUF / ONNX / TensorRT / Hugging Face / Docker) → deployment versions with promote / rollback and an on-demand drift check. vLLM is a deployment runner, not an export format.

Audit spine: imports, document uploads, training starts and dispatch errors, eval runs, exports and deployment actions emit a RunEvent with stage, structured payload, and (on errors) a reason code from a fixed taxonomy. Same stream feeds the run timeline and failure clusters on Ship → Monitor, and the support bundle.

Common first questions

Quick answers; the long version lives on the FAQs page

Is BrewSLM open source?

Yes. Source lives at github.com/TensorGreed/__SLM__. Run it locally; no account or hosted service required.

Do I need a GPU?

For training generative models, in practice yes. BrewSLM targets small language models: up to ~10B parameters; the Academy course uses 135M. A 24 GB consumer GPU handles LoRA up to about 7B with gradient checkpointing and short sequences; a 10B model is about 20 GB of bf16 weights alone, so it needs a larger card (the memory table in Academy Lesson 1.15 shows the arithmetic). Encoder taggers (DeBERTa) train on CPU. Ingest and export need no GPU; eval runs on CPU, slowly.

Where does my data go?

Into the project's local directory on your machine. SQLite metadata, JSONL row storage, file artifacts. Your data leaves only when you point a model (the data writer for synthetic generation, an LLM judge, or an answer-key drafter) at a hosted endpoint; local Ollama works for all three. Downloads from Hugging Face, Kaggle, git or web sources and a Hub publish also use the network.

Can I plug in a custom mapper for my weird dataset?

Yes. Drop a Python module under DATASET_MAPPER_PLUGIN_MODULES; it registers via register_dataset_mappers(register) alongside the built-ins. Same pattern as data-adapter and training-runtime plugins.

Quickstart

Clone, install, train a demo

Six blocks. The first four boot the platform; the last two are the demo run-through. Match this against the README for the canonical version.

# 1. Clone

$ git clone https://github.com/TensorGreed/__SLM__ brewslm && cd brewslm

 

# 2. Backend (Python 3.11+)

$ cd backend && python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

$ pip install -r requirements.txt && cp .env.example .env

$ uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000

# once, after this first boot creates the tables: alembic stamp head

 

# 3. Redis + the training worker (new shell). Without them Train never runs.

$ redis-server & # or any Redis on localhost:6379

$ cd backend && source .venv/bin/activate

$ celery -A app.worker.celery_app worker --pool=threads --concurrency=2

 

# 4. Frontend (new shell; Node 20.19+ or 22.12+)

$ cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev

 

# 5. Open http://localhost:5173, log in as admin with the API_KEY from

# backend/.env (sk-mock-admin-key), then "+ New Project" or a starter project

 

# 6. Open demo "Demo · Support FAQ" → Train → Train → Launch, then watch the

# bell and the worker log. Your own data: upload documents on Data → Sources,

# or import a labelled dataset (see Capabilities → Importing datasets).
